Old man take: I like Olivia Rodrigo for what she is - she’s a very talented performer - but she’s a Disney child star making corporate music.

She may make overtures toward authenticity or garnish her music with references that signal street cred but at the end of the day, it’s pop. That’s not a dig on pop - in its own way, making pop music with broad appeal is even harder than making poetic indie rock for art school dropouts - but because it is made to target as many people as possible, the pintrest board aesthetic is just part of the bargain.

text:
I like that record a lot, but there are a few points in this that I'd push back on.

First, I've never heard anyone say that no one in the band could play. Vicious famously couldn't play very well, and never really learned. McLaren put him in the band specifically because he fit the image, not because he had any talent.

No disagreement about Jones and Cook's playing, though. They really do sound great on the record. And I love a lot of the songs you mentioned, especially EMI and No Feelings.

The "boy band" critique is perhaps a bit overstated, but I don't think it's unreasonable, given McLaren's level of control over the membership (as evidenced, again, by hiring a bassist who died before he really learned to play bass). It's an iconic record that did a lot to shape the sound of punk as a genre, but it's kind of tough to square the Sex Pistols with the way the ethos of punk later developed. These weren't four punk kids who wanted to make a band together. It was four kids thrown into a band together, in no small part based on image, in order to explicitly attempt to capitalize on a sound popular in New York and bring it to London.

John Lydon's later political about face doesn't help things for the band. As good of a song as Anarchy in the UK is, it's a bit hard to take seriously if you know that the guy who's singing later became a vocal supporter of Brexit and Donald Trump.

“Ode To Billie Joe” by Bobbie Gentry was originally the B-side to “Mississippi Delta”, but the cryptic story of “Billie Joe” caught the ears of listeners.

“Green Onions” by Booker T. & The MGs was originally the B-side of “Behave Yourself” and was first released on Stax’s sister label Volt Records. Once “Green Onions” started gaining traction, the record was reissued on the Stax label with “Onions” as the A-side.

The next few examples are all Sun Records releases.

“I Walk The Line” by Johnny Cash was the B-side to “Get Rhythm”. This “B-side” would gain Sun Records its 2nd million seller.

“I Forgot To Remember To Forget” by Elvis Presley was the B-side to “Mystery Train”. “Mystery Train” was a decent hit itself, but “I Forgot To Remember To Forget” became Elvis’ first #1 hit.

“Just Walkin’ In The Rain” by The Prisonaires was the B-side to “Baby Please”. “Baby Please”, with its rocking electric guitar by Joe Hill Louis, was definitely the more typical Sun Records song, but the Ink Spots inspired charm of “Just Walkin’ In The Rain” was the song that charmed the record buying public.

“Folsom Prison Blues” by Johnny Cash was the B-side of “So Doggone Lonesome”. This one is an unusual example, because “So Doggone Lonesome” was the bigger hit upon initial release. I was a tween at the time of Saturday Night Fever. Loved it, like most of my classmates. Managed to get in to see the movie, which was strictly for ages 18+ where I lived, no exceptions for adult accompaniment. Then came the "disco sucks" backlash and no, I don't think it was all about the Bee Gees, Saturday Night Fever or white/hetero crossover artists, though they were definitely part of it.

IMO it was mainly about the chart dominance of singles that are now considered corny, fad dances like The Hustle, and as you say racism and homophobia -- Black artists, increasing visibility of gay people through nightlife culture (especially fashion). It was all too much fun, not serious enough, not deep like Floyd or Bruce. You couldn't just sit and listen, you had to get up and dance. Ugh.

I really regret having got caught up in it. Led me to dismiss a lot of great music over the years. I think the disco-sucks attitude took pretty deep root in me because of my impressionable age and having older siblings who largely shaped my taste with classic rock then New Wave.

So it was all kind of sad, but in hindsight there were some funny, or maybe just hypocritical, aspects.

Many of us did gold-medal mental gymnastics to deny that a song like "Heart of Glass" is a disco song. No, no, Blondie is a New Wave band therefore it's a New Wave song! Debbie Harry was far too hot to cancel.

Is that the Stones doing disco on the Some Girls album, especially the hit single "Beast of Burden"? No, not really, this is just a little funky that's all. Then they had a couple of undeniable full-fledged disco songs on the followup (Emotional Rescue) and, well, that album sucks, right?

Lots of people, including myself, flat-out refused to see the connections between blues, funk, Motown and disco and understand why disco was actually a perfectly reasonable avenue for a band like the Stones to explore.

Still, the Stones were not caught in the backlash despite the obvious disco influences on Some Girls, and Emotional Rescue came after the backlash. Which could be seen as a statement: "disco sucks" sucks.

Was a teen unable to get into see Saturday Night Fever in the theater when it was out, but the soundtrack was undeniable at the time and still holds up as a snapshot in time today. The Bee Gees (and Andy Gibb too) at the time dominated the charts, but a lot of other songs at the time were big hits -- A Fifth of Beethoven, If I Can't Have You, Manhattan Skyline all played heavily on the radio. KC & The Sunshine Band were huge. So many acts came after too, too many to name -- but Rod Stewart, Rolling Stones, KISS famously went disco too. Heck, listen to Paul McCartney during this time. Black acts were well accepted by the disco crowd, it was very open.

I think at the time, we had come out of the 60s and protests and post-Vietnam, people I think just wanted to relax and have F-U-N. Party. Although I was too young for the clubs, they were hugely popular, people just wanted to dance after coming out of a lot of grim times. Our family danced to the SNF soundtrack just like everyone else was doing.

Rock was there too and influenced (as the other poster suggested) influenced by disco, and danceable rock was around in bands like Blondie and David Bowie and even Devo. It was an incredibly creative time. You could even say hair bands later tried to balance the fun aspect of disco but keep the rock intact, some with more success than others.

The Disco Sucks movement came more out of the huge popularity of disco eclipsing old school Rock and Roll for a short while. A lot of people felt threatened by the frivolity of the music, and probably some of the fashion as well. I can't accurately describe how dominant disco was on the airwaves for a while there, and I am sure a lot of more serious and harder-edged rock acts and fans felt like their music was getting pushed out by all the "silliness." In truth, they both existed fine side-by-side. I mean Heart's Barracuda was a huge FM radio hit and Zeppelin was enormously popular as well.

For me personally, the whole Disco Demolition thing was barely a blip on the radar. I don't even remember it occurring, and I think most people would say the same -- maybe some hardcore rock fans remember it better. I think disco didn't end because of that, but rather that the genre kinda burned itself out from overexposure, and Punk and New Wave were coming through. People were interested in serious topics again. It was a cycle like any other.

Today, I think people look back fondly on the disco era as a creative and unique time, and it doesn't get near as much hate because it's just a style of music like any other.

Disco was everywhere. I was a little kid, nine years old, and I remember the book club catalog being saturated with disco-related books. It was on TV and my mom — out of the target age range — went to dance exercise classes, all disco. Disco was relatively cheap to produce and didn't create monster performers (like the Rolling Stones) that needed tours, publishing, the whole apparatus. The industry loved it for that reason.

The topline popular content was safe for popular consumption — no weird or challenging subject matter, at least explicitly. Mostly sex songs that sounded like love songs, or instrumentals. The Top 40 stuff wasn't coded as black or Hispanic or queer. Even the Village People seemed like a fun bunch of guys who dressed up in costumes — YMCA was just a song about a great place to hang out, right? The challenging stuff stayed in the clubs.

And plenty of rock acts dipped their toes in — the Stones, KISS, Alice Cooper, Queen, even the Dead. They did their four-on-the-floor thing and nobody burned their records over it.

I think what actually killed disco at the pop level was oversaturation and corniness — and the Bee Gees were ground zero for both. By 1979 it had become a self-parody, and that happens to any genre that gets strip-mined by the industry. Disco Demolition Night is kind of a red herring anyway — it was a very specific Chicago phenomenon, bound up in the decline of local rock radio and a particular strain of Midwest radio-jock grievance. Steve Dahl wasn't leading a cultural revolution. He was fighting a format war.

The racism and homophobia were real, but they may have been more undertow than engine. The pop version of disco had already whitewashed and straightened itself into the mainstream — and then bloated itself to death there.

And of course disco didn't die — it went back underground and became house music. Chicago, same city as Disco Demolition Night. Make of that what you will.

text:
I've said it on here before, the exaggeration and mythologization of the 'Disco Sucks' thing - which was mostly the work of a single 'shock' DJ - has been part of the construction of the corporate apologia 'Poptimism' narrative, which is broadly concerned with linking the multicultural experience of Pop music as positive propaganda for the monopolized entertainment sector brought about through neoliberalism. The transition to neoliberalism starts halfway through Jimmy Carter's term, when he brought in the first wave of Third Way advocates, so it only makes sense that it would align with the peak of the Disco craze.

I like a lot of Disco - those Bee Gees tracks still sound great, and turned me on to all the earlier Bee Gees pre-Disco work (their late 60s psychedelic pop is terrific, and Robin Gibb's 1970 solo album rules) - and I've always liked KC and the Sunshine Band and like a bunch of Disco/Rock crossover tracks, and lot of that era of Italian electronic music that intertwines with Disco. In general, I think Funk is a way more interesting dance-oriented 70s art movement, but I certainly don't think 'Disco sucks.'

BUT, it was extremely overplayed back when there were far less ways to hear new music, which had the effect of artists in other genres having to adopt the sound if they wanted to get airplay. There were disco remixes of everything because it was such a generic sound that is could be slapped under anything for a hit - Pac-Man, Star Wars, Mickey Mouse, you name it (note the synthesis with corporate IP, btw).

While Disco, and specifically the club scene that surrounded it, was largely driven by gay and minority communities in the big cities, most of the people hearing it had no connection to that, and - like you said - were mostly exposed to it through straight white performers (including the Rock bands 'going disco'). Saturday Night Fever is about a straight Italian guy struggling with depression, right? While it's inevitable that some of the reactionary response to Disco was driven by racism, misogyny, or homophobia, I suspect it has more to do with a broader anti-urban sentiment on one front, and anti-corporate-art sentiment on another.

Clearly, the Rock guys (broadly) had no problem with black artists - if anything, they venerated them - and this is the era of gender-bending Glam Rock and rock gods Bowie, Jagger, and Marc Bolan talking about being bisexual in interviews, and most people knowing about megastars Elton John and Freddie Mercury being gay. This was all part of the 60s sexual liberation via Rock music thing - most people who were listening to Rock music, a massive mainstream genre, in the late 70s weren't Ted Nugent-like chuds. They were listening to Fleetwood Mac and Peter Frampton and the like.

In short, I think the quick end of the Disco era was mostly from extreme over-saturation, not from bigotry.
